messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 34
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Firefighter
- Trauma Type: Relief worker in war zone
- Pcl5: 40

As a firefighter, he had seen his share of burning buildings and mangled cars, but nothing prepared him for the sounds of a city without a roof. When his unit volunteered for a six-month relief deployment to a war-torn region, he went because he believed he could help. He believed in the skill-set he had honed for a decade: controlled breathing, situational awareness, the ability to move toward danger while others moved away. He thought it would translate.

It did not.

In the first week, his convoy hit a crater where a road used to be. He remembers the dust settling in his mouth, the taste of grit and gasoline. He helped carry a man whose leg had been torn open by shrapnel. The man’s wife followed them, screaming a language he could not understand but whose meaning he knew perfectly. He put pressure on the wound. The man looked at him with an expression he still cannot name—relief, terror, or accusation. The man died before the helicopter arrived.

He does not talk about the children. He told me once, in a flat voice, that there was a playground that had been hit. He stopped talking about that part of the deployment three sessions ago. I do not push. Instead I notice how his hands tighten on his knees when he says, “I did my job.”

When he came home, his wife said he seemed different. He did not feel different; he felt *gone*. The first time he returned to the fire station, the alarm bell sent him under the kitchen table before he could think. His crew laughed it off as a joke. He laughed too, because laughing was easier than explaining that for three seconds he was back in that convoy, hearing the thud of an explosion that had not happened yet. He started sleeping in the living room because his wife’s breathing at night sounded like someone counting down.

His PCL-5 score of 40 reflects what he has known for months: he is not fine. He re-experiences the worst moments during quiet moments at the station—a sudden whiff of diesel, the crackle of a radio, the way a certain colour of dust settles on the engine bay floor. He avoids news coverage of the conflict. He avoids pictures of sand. He avoids the international section of the grocery store because the packaging reminds him of a market he drove past every day. He stopped volunteering for the big calls. His captain noticed. He told the captain he had a bad back.

Marriage has become a series of near-misses. He does not want to fight, so he agrees to everything. His wife says he is not present. She is right. He is somewhere else, standing in a dust cloud, trying to remember what it felt like to believe that the world was a place where children played in playgrounds.

He came to therapy because his wife said he scared her when he woke up screaming. She said he looked at her like she was a stranger. He does not remember those moments. But he remembers the dust, the taste of it, and the man’s eyes. He remembers thinking, *I am supposed to be the one who helps.* Now he is not sure what he is supposed to be.

He still goes to work. He still puts on the gear. But inside the helmet, the noise of the city sounds like the noise of a city that is about to disappear.
